Unit 10: Binary Logic & Circuits

SL curriculum overview and structured learning plan.

Introduction

How do simple switches create complex logic?

This unit bridges the gap between raw mathematics and physical hardware. You will learn how computers quantify the world using Binary, how simple Logic Gates perform decisions, and how the Operating System manages these resources to let you run multiple programs at once.

You'll start with the basics of data representation (Integers, Hex, ASCII, Images). Then you'll build Logic Circuits and simplify them using Karnaugh Maps. Finally, you'll explore how the OS acts as a manager, scheduling tasks and handling hardware Interrupts.

Data Representation

Computers only understand 'On' and 'Off'. We use this to represent everything:

  • Numbers: Binary (Base-2) and Hexadecimal (Base-16).
  • Text: ASCII (English only) vs Unicode (Global languages).
  • Media: Bitmaps (Pixels/Color Depth) and Digital Audio (Sampling).
Logic Gates & Circuits

The building blocks of the CPU. We combine gates to create logic:

  • Basic Gates: AND, OR, NOT.
  • Universal Gates: NAND, NOR (Can build anything).
  • Exclusive Gates: XOR, XNOR.
  • Karnaugh Maps: A graphical way to simplify complex Boolean logic.
The Operating System

Hardware is useless without software to manage it. The OS handles:

  • Process Management: Scheduling who gets the CPU (Round Robin, FCFS).
  • Memory Management: Using Virtual Memory and Paging.
  • Peripheral Management: Using Drivers and Interrupts.
Key Terminology
TermDefinition
Hexadecimal A base-16 number system (0-9, A-F) used to simplify binary representation for humans.
Two's Complement A method of representing negative integers in binary where the most significant bit is a negative value.
Unicode (UTF-8) A character encoding standard capable of representing all characters in all writing systems of the world.
Logic Gate A physical device implementing a Boolean function (e.g., AND, OR).
Truth Table A table showing all possible input combinations and their corresponding outputs.
Karnaugh Map (K-Map) A method to simplify boolean algebra expressions using a grid where adjacent cells differ by only one bit.
Operating System (OS) System software that manages computer hardware and software resources and provides common services for programs.
Scheduling The method by which the OS decides which process runs on the CPU and for how long.
Interrupt A signal to the CPU indicating an event that needs immediate attention.
Virtual Memory Using secondary storage (Hard Drive) to act as temporary RAM when main memory is full.
